metadata.title: Miɗo Waawi Pular! — Competences 1–3 Curriculum
metadata.source_book: Miɗo Waawi Pular! Learner's Guide to Pular (Fuuta Jallon), 2nd Edition
metadata.orthography: UNESCO Bamako 1966 harmonized alphabet (implosives: ɓ, ɗ, ƴ; palatal: ñ; velar: ŋ)

key_points: Pular is written phonetically (one symbol, one sound) using the 1966 UNESCO Bamako orthography.
Five pure vowels (a, e, i, o, u) pronounced like Spanish or Italian; double vowels (aa, ee, ii, oo, uu) mark vowel length.
Three implosive consonants: ɓ (bh), ɗ (dh), and ƴ (yh). Contrasting normal vs. implosive consonants changes word meaning.
Double consonants (bb, cc, tt) indicate stressed/geminated consonants; ' marks a glottal stop.
c is pronounced like 'ch' in 'cello'; ñ is pronounced 'ny'; ŋ is pronounced like 'ng' in 'sing'; r is rolled.

cultural_notes.title: Respect
cultural_notes.summary: Older people, authority figures, and strangers are addressed in the plural (On jaraama). Respect also uses plural forms in the 3rd person and special respect vocabulary (e.g., ɓelagol instead of waalugol for sleeping).

cultural_notes.title: Body Language
cultural_notes.summary: Shaking hands with both hands, or holding your forearm/elbow while shaking hands, shows deference. Looking downward or away is respectful; direct eye contact can be read as aggressive.

cultural_notes.title: Greetings During Prayertime
cultural_notes.summary: Elders walking with prayer beads and moving lips cannot interrupt prayer; greet them with a smile, nod, or hands clasped in front of your chest.

cultural_notes.title: The Will of God
cultural_notes.summary: Si Alla jaɓi ('God willing', literally 'If God accepts') accompanies virtually any statement or arrangement about the future.

lines.speaker: Susan
lines.english: Yes. I am a Math teacher.

lines.speaker: Salyu
lines.pular: Ko Bah mi yettetee. An le?
lines.english: My last name is Bah. And you?

lines.speaker: Ousmane
lines.pular: Min ko Ousmane Diallo mi innetee. Ko mo a honto?
lines.english: My name is Ousmane Diallo. Where are you from?

lines.speaker: Salyu
lines.pular: Ko mo mi Labe. An, ko honto iwuɗaa?
lines.english: I'm from Labé. And you, where do you come from?

lines.speaker: Ousmane
lines.pular: Tigi tigi, ko Besseko mi iwi.

lines.speaker: Ousmane
lines.pular: Ko yettude Alla. Ko honɗun gollataa?
lines.english: Thanks be to God. What work do you do?

lines.speaker: Salyu
lines.pular: Ko mi jannoowo Anglee. An kadi, ko a jannoowo?
lines.english: I am an English teacher. Are you also a teacher?

key_points: No grammatical gender in 3rd person singular: o means both 'he' and 'she' (independent: kanko).
Two forms of 'we': exclusive men / menen (excludes the listener) and inclusive en / enen (includes the listener).
2nd person plural on / onon also serves as the polite/respectful singular 'you'.
The particle ko fills in for 'to be' in equative/focused statements (Ko mi jannoowo — 'I am a teacher').
The negation of ko is wonaa (Wonaa mi jannoowo — 'I am not a teacher').
Marriage expressions differ by gender: men use A jombii? / Mi jombaali. / Mi jombii.; women use A jombaama? / Mi jombaaka. / Mi jombaama.

cultural_notes.title: Last Name Games (Sanakuyaagal)
cultural_notes.summary: Among the four noble Fulɓe-Fuuta clans, joking relationships (sanakuyaagal) pair Diallo with Balde/Bah, and Sow with Barry. Cross-clan pairs playfully tease each other on sight.

cultural_notes.title: Marriage Proposals
cultural_notes.summary: Casual marriage proposals (Miɗo faala jombude ma) are frequently made in jest and are best met with humor or polite deflections (e.g., Miɗo mari moodi — 'I have a husband', or Mi yettaama — 'I'm already taken').

lines.speaker: Host
lines.pular: Ko Buubakar o innete. Ko men neenegotooɓe.
lines.english: His name is Boubacar. We have the same mother (we are full siblings).

lines.speaker: Visitor
lines.english: How many younger siblings do you have?

key_points: Possessive pronouns follow the noun they modify: 'baaba an' (my father), 'ɓeyngu maa' (your wife).
A person's name can directly replace the possessive pronoun after the noun: 'baaba Aamadu' (Amadou's father), 'ɓeyngu Yunuusa' (Younoussa's wife).
The 1st-person plural inclusive ('men') and 2nd-person plural ('mon') possessive pronouns have lengthened, more insistent forms: 'me'en' and 'mo'on'.
Numbers differ slightly when counting people vs. things/animals (e.g., 'duuɓi tati' = 3 years vs. 'Amerikenɓe tato' = 3 Americans; 'jelu' = how many things vs. 'njelo' = how many people).
Compound numbers link tens and units with 'e' (e.g., 'sappo e ɗiɗi' = 12, 'nogay e jeetati' = 28, 'cappande tati e tati' = 33).
The key word 'woo' introduces reported speech or hearsay ('he/she says...' or 'they say...'), e.g., 'Woo, o waawataa Pular.' ('He says he doesn't speak Pular.').

cultural_notes.title: Family Terminology
cultural_notes.summary: Kinship words like brother, father, mother, uncle, and child are applied broadly in Fulɓe society. A 'brother' may be a half-brother, cousin, distant relative, or close friend; establishing exact genealogy requires asking whether two people share the same mother (neenegooto) or father (baabagooto).

cultural_notes.title: Polygamy
cultural_notes.summary: Many men have two, three, or four wives, creating specific everyday terms for co-wives (siinaa) and half-siblings who share a father but have different mothers (baabagooto).

cultural_notes.title: Age
cultural_notes.summary: Traditionally, birthdates are not emphasized in Fulɓe culture, so it is common for people not to know their exact numerical age.

vocabulary.usage_note: Standard greeting and expression of thanks used with peers or younger people.
Used when greeting elders, authority figures, strangers, or two or more people.

vocabulary.english: Is there no evil? (Is everything OK?)
vocabulary.usage_note: Core follow-up greeting question; standard reply is 'Jam tun.' Add 'ton' (there) or 'gaa' (here) for location.
The universal positive reply to almost all Pular greeting questions.
Informal greeting commonly used among young people; features a glottal stop (').
Borrowed from French 'marcher'. Common replies: 'No marsude fota.' (very well) or 'No marsude seeɗa.' (so-so).
Answered with 'Jam tun.' or 'Hiɓe e jam.' (They are well).

vocabulary.english: Did you sleep in peace? (Good morning)
vocabulary.usage_note: Respectful morning greeting; familiar equivalent is 'A walli e jam?' / 'A waali e jam?'.
Common alternative response to 'Jam tun.', similar to 'Alhamdullilahi.'.
Uses the inclusive pronoun 'en' (you and I).
Often answered with 'En jango, si Alla jaɓi.'
Literally 'If God accepts'; standard caveat when making plans or saying goodbye.
Standard affirmative in Fuuta Jallon; 'Eyyo.' is also heard in northern Fuuta Jallon and Senegal.
Also 'O'owooye.' Distinguish the crisp glottal stop in 'O'o' (no) from the drawn-out intonation of 'Oo-o!' (bye!).
Essential beginner phrase when people comment on your Pular.
Reply with 'Ko [Name] mi innete.' Synonym: 'Ko honno wi'eteɗa?' or short form 'Innde maa?'.
Short form: 'Yettoore maa?'. Reply with 'Ko [Last Name] mi yettetee.'.
Reply with 'Ko [Place] mi iwi.' (e.g., 'Ko Amerik mi iwi.').
Reply with 'Ko mo mi [Place].' (e.g., 'Ko mo mi Labe.' or 'Ko mo mi Dakar.').

vocabulary.english: What do you do? (What is your work?)
vocabulary.usage_note: Reply with 'Ko mi [occupation].' (e.g., 'Ko mi jannoowo.').
Reply with 'Ko [Place] mi hoɗi.' (e.g., 'Ko Maamu mi hoɗi.').

vocabulary.english: is not / am not (negation of ko)
vocabulary.usage_note: Negates equative sentences formed with 'ko' (e.g., 'Wonaa mi Faranseejo.' — 'I am not French.'). Also heard as wanaa, hinaa, or naa.
Notice the double 'n' (jannoowo = teacher) contrasting with single 'n' (jangoowo = student).
Synonym: 'lekkoljo' (pl. 'lekkolɓe').
Related Pular word for healer/doctor: 'ñawndoowo' (pl. 'ñawndooɓe').
Featured in the taxi-park dialogue; related word 'yeeyoowo' means seller.
Common occupation across the Fuuta Jallon.
'Pullo-Fuuta' (pl. 'Fulɓe-Fuuta') specifically refers to a Guinean Peuhl from the Fuuta Jallon.
Irregular initial consonant alternation from singular 'g-' to plural 'w-'.
Irregular initial consonant alternation from singular 'd-' to plural 'r-'.
Respectful form: 'ben' (or 'ɓen'). Father's older brother is 'ɓen mawɗo'.
Respectful form: 'yuuma' / 'yumma'. Use 3rd-person plural 'hiɓe' when referring to a mother or father respectfully.
Singular full form is 'kotiraawo'; generic/address form is 'koto'.
Example: 'Adama Hawa ko jaaja an.' ('Adama Hawa is my older sister.').
Gender-neutral term for any younger sibling.
Distinct from paternal uncles: 'bappa' (father's younger brother) and 'ɓen mawɗo' (father's older brother).
Father's sister (paternal aunt) is 'yaaye' / 'yaaya'.
Pairs with 'pati' (grandmother) and 'taanira' (grandchild).
Used for both maternal and paternal grandmothers.
Related to 'ɓeynguure nden' (nuclear family: wives and children). Co-wife is 'siinaa'.
Also used as a respectful title for a learned or older man (e.g., Moodi Aliu).
Refers to offspring/descendants (unlike 'paykun', which refers to a young child by age).
Contrasts with 'baabagooto' (pl. 'baabagotooɓe'), meaning half-sibling (same father, different mothers).
Reply with 'Ko [Name/Relation] nii.' (e.g., 'Ko koto an nii.' — 'That is my older brother.').
Literally 'How many years do you have?'. Reply: 'Ko duuɓi [number] mi mari.'.

exercises.prompt: Vowel length and consonant stress change meaning in Pular. Which word in this minimal triplet means 'there is none'?
exercises.explanation: 'Alla' (stressed ll) means God, 'aala' (long initial aa) means tool, and 'alaa' (long final aa) means 'there is none' (as in 'Tanna alaa?').

exercises.prompt: How does the implosive consonant 'ƴ' change the meaning between 'yettugol' and 'ƴettugol'?

options.text: yettugol = to greet; ƴettugol = to take
yettugol = to take; ƴettugol = to greet
yettugol = to wait; ƴettugol = to climb
They are spelling variants with the same meaning

exercises.explanation: Regular 'y' in 'yettugol' means 'to greet / thank', whereas implosive 'ƴ' in 'ƴettugol' means 'to take'.

exercises.prompt: Match each Pular greeting or leave-taking expression with its closest English equivalent.

pairs.right: Have you spent the day in peace?

exercises.explanation: These six phrases cover the complete arc of a Pular greeting: opening check-in, peace reply, time-of-day inquiry, and farewell.

exercises.prompt: Translate into respectful Pular: 'Good morning.' (Literally: 'Did you sleep in peace?')
exercises.explanation: 'On belike e jam?' uses both the respectful plural pronoun 'on' and the respect verb 'ɓelagol' (to sleep).

exercises.prompt: Translate into Pular: 'How is work going?'
exercises.explanation: From Dialogue 2 ('Salminagol sukaajo'): 'Golle ɗen no marsude?' asks how work is going; the short form 'Golle ɗen?' is also used.

exercises.source_reference: Competence 1, Exercise D (Fill in the blanks)
exercises.prompt: Fill in the missing words to complete this greeting exchange.
exercises.template:
A: A jaraama.
B: A jaraama. Tanna {{1}}?
A: {{2}} tun. An le?
B: Jam tun. Ɓeyngure nden {{3}} e jam?
A: Jam tun. Golle ɗen no {{4}}?
B: No marsude seeɗa. Awa, en ñalorma.
A: Awa, en ñalorma, si {{5}} {{6}}.
exercises.explanation: Standard Pular exchanges pair 'Tanna alaa?' with 'Jam tun.', use 'no' for stative/locative predicates ('no e jam', 'no marsude'), and close future plans with 'si Alla jaɓi'.

exercises.prompt: You are greeting an elderly man in the village. Which greeting and body language are most respectful?

options.text: Say 'A jaraama, mawɗo!' while maintaining firm, direct eye contact.
Say 'On jaraama, mawɓe.' while shaking with both hands (or holding your forearm) and looking slightly down or away.
Say 'No wa'i?' and wave from across the path without slowing down.
Say 'Oo-o!' and shake briskly with your left hand.

exercises.explanation: Elders are addressed in the plural ('On jaraama, mawɓe.'). Supporting your handshake with your other hand and averting direct eye contact show deference in Fulɓe culture.

exercises.source_reference: Competence 2, Exercise A (Getting to know you)
exercises.prompt: Complete the introductory conversation between Susan and Alfa.
exercises.template:
Alfa: Ko honno {{1}}?
Susan: Ko Susan mi {{2}}. An le?
Alfa: Ko Alfa mi innete. Ko a Amerikeenjo?
Susan: Hii-hi, {{3}} mi Amerikeenjo.
Alfa: Ko a jannoowo?
Susan: O'o, {{4}} mi jannoowo. Ko mi dofturjo.
exercises.explanation: Use 'ko' for affirmative identification ('ko mi Amerikeenjo') and 'wonaa' to negate it ('wonaa mi jannoowo').

exercises.prompt: Answer the question first in the affirmative, then in the negative (switching the pronoun correctly): 'An, ko a Pullo-Fuuta?'
exercises.explanation: A question addressed to 'an / a' (you, singular) is answered with 'mi' (I). 'ko' flips to 'wonaa' in the negative.

exercises.prompt: Answer in the affirmative and negative (speaking for your group to an outsider): 'Onon, ko on Amerikeenɓe?'
exercises.explanation: Because the speaker is answering 'you all' (onon/on) and excluding the person who asked the question, the exclusive 'we' pronoun 'men' is required.

exercises.prompt: You and your American colleague are speaking to a Guinean host. How do you say 'We are from America'?
exercises.explanation: Use exclusive 'men' because the Guinean listener is NOT included in 'we'. Inclusive 'en' would mean 'you and I both'.

exercises.prompt: Connect each Pular introduction question with its matching answer.
exercises.explanation: Notice how each question mirrors the verb or structure in the answer: inneteɗaa -> innete, yetteteɗaa -> yettete, jombaama -> jombaaka (for women), jombii -> jombii (for men).

exercises.prompt: Translate into Pular: 'I am not a doctor.'
exercises.explanation: Replace 'ko' with 'wonaa' before the subject pronoun 'mi' and the singular noun 'dofturjo' (doctor).

exercises.prompt: Translate into Pular: 'They are teachers.'
exercises.explanation: Both the pronoun ('ɓe' = they) and the occupation noun ('jannooɓe' = teachers, plural of 'jannoowo') take the human plural form.

exercises.prompt: Which pair correctly asks a WOMAN if she is married and gives her negative response ('No, I am not married')?
exercises.explanation: In Pular, marriage verbs use the active voice for men ('A jombii?' / 'Mi jombaali.') and the passive voice for women ('A jombaama?' / 'Mi jombaaka.').

exercises.source_reference: Competence 3, Exercise A (Fun with numbers, part 1, #4)
exercises.prompt: Write the number 29 in Pular (using the standard counting form for things/years).
exercises.explanation: 'nogay' is 20, 'e' links tens and units, and 'jeenay' is 9.

exercises.prompt: Pular uses distinct number forms when counting people versus things or time. Which pair is correct for 'three Americans' and 'three years'?
exercises.explanation: Counting people takes the '-o' ending ('tato', and 'njelo' for 'how many'), while counting things, animals, or years uses 'tati' (and 'jelu' for 'how many').

exercises.source_reference: Competence 3, Vocabulary (Family Members) & Exercise D (Family ties)
exercises.prompt: Match each Pular family relationship term with its exact English meaning.
exercises.explanation: Fulɓe kinship terms distinguish age among siblings (koto/jaaja vs. miñan) and maternal vs. paternal uncles and aunts (kaawu vs. bappa/yaaye).

exercises.source_reference: Competence 3, Exercise B (How's the wife and kids?, #5 & #10)
exercises.prompt: Someone asks 'Honno neene Sulayman waɗi?' ('How is Sulayman's mother doing?'). Which response uses the proper respectful pronoun?
exercises.explanation: When referring to a parent or elder in the 3rd person, Pular uses the plural pronoun 'hiɓe' ('they are well') out of respect rather than singular 'himo'.

exercises.prompt: How do you report what someone else said or what you heard: '(They say) he has twenty children'?
exercises.explanation: The particle 'woo' precedes reported speech or hearsay ('he says / they say'), and 'nogayo' is the people-counting form of 20.

exercises.source_reference: Competence 3, Exercise H (Fill in the blanks)
exercises.prompt: Fill in the blanks to complete this conversation about family members.
exercises.template:
A: Ko {{1}} ɓen maa innetee?
B: Ɓen an ko Aamadu innetee.
A: Ko honno neene {{2}} innetee?
B: Yumma {{3}} ko Aysata innetee.
A: Ko kotiraaɓe {{4}} maruɗaa?
B: Ko kotiraawo {{5}} mi mari.
exercises.explanation: Possessive pronouns follow the noun ('neene maa' = your mother, 'yumma an' = my mother); 'njelo' asks 'how many' for people, and 'gooto' means 'one' person.

exercises.prompt: Translate into Pular: 'I am twenty-eight years old.'
exercises.answer: Ko duuɓi nogay e jeetati mi mari.
accepted_answers: Ko duuɓi nogay e jeetati mi mari.
Ko duubi nogay e jeetati mi mari.
Ko duuɓi nogay e jeetati mi mari
Miɗo mari duuɓi nogay e jeetati.
exercises.explanation: Age is expressed with 'duuɓi' (years) + the things-counting number ('nogay e jeetati' = 28) + 'marugol' (to have): literally 'It is 28 years that I have.'

exercises.prompt: Translate into Pular: 'Karim's mother is a cook.'
exercises.explanation: To show possession by a named person, place the name right after the noun ('Neene Karim' = Karim's mother), then link to the occupation with 'ko' ('ko defoowo').
